title: The ozone hole
what: Ozone over the whole Earth each October since 1970, the Antarctic ozone hole an opening in it; from 2003, the ozone layer as a surface round the Earth each day from July to December; the hole’s area each spring since 1979, and the ozone-depleting gases over Antarctica since 1992. The Montreal Protocol (1987) is marked.
how: The globe shows the month’s mean of total ozone in October, when the Antarctic hole is deepest, from the MSR-2 reanalysis: blue at 220 Dobson units through pale grey to red at 400, as the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service colours it. Under 220, the line that marks the hole, the sheet is left open to the Earth beneath. A reanalysis takes satellite measurements, corrected against ground stations, into a model of the air’s ozone: from 1979 it has no gaps, and where no satellite saw (the polar night) its values are the model’s. Before 1979 it rests on one early instrument that saw less each year: those Octobers are coarser and have gaps, drawn grey, never filled, and 1977 and 1978, with values for under a tenth of the Earth, are left out. Each map is thinned from half a degree to one. While a map is fetched, and if it cannot be, the hole is drawn as a cap of its mean area round the South Pole: the real hole wanders and stretches off the pole. The area beside the globe is NASA’s, the mean of each day’s hole from 7 September to 13 October; a month’s mean map shows a smaller one, since the hole moves from day to day. NASA’s record has no 1995: no satellite measured the hole each day. On a day from 1 July to 31 December of 2003 to 2025 the globe shows instead the ozone layer as a surface round the Earth, after the way the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service draws the ozone hole: where the partial pressure of ozone is 12 mPa, its lower and upper sides, coloured by total ozone, from the CAMS reanalysis at 12:00 UT. Where no height holds that much ozone there is no surface: over Antarctica in spring that opening is the hole, wider than the area under 220 Dobson units. The partial pressure is worked out from ozone’s mixing ratio on ten pressure levels from 200 to 5 hPa, three to five kilometres apart, so the surface’s heights are no finer than that; a level’s height is taken as 7 km for each fall of the pressure by e, within about a kilometre of the true one. The surface is every three degrees, smoothed between, and its heights are drawn 40 times larger than life, or the layer, a few kilometres thick, could not be told from the ground. While the layer is on, the bar at the foot is ozone’s own: it reaches only the years there is data for, 1970 to 2025, and plays a year at a step through the Octobers and a day at a step through each season.
